title: Stop at the match cap?
hook: Is the employer-match threshold also the right personal savings target?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Distinguish the incentive schedule's kink from a complete retirement decision.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Distinguish the incentive schedule's kink from a complete retirement decision.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: A toy employer matches 50% of contributions only up to €60. You contribute €80. What does the employer add? Toy inputs A=[80, 60, 0.5]; B=[40, 60, 0.5].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[30, 110, 20], [20, 60, 0]]. Labels: Employer €, Total saved €, Above cap €.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: The capped schedule stops adding employer money above the matching threshold. The contrast stays below the cap. This kink explains the displayed marginal incentive, while a complete retirement decision also needs preferences and other constraints.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses Contribution €=40, Match cap €=60, Match fraction=0.5. What is Employer €? Answer: 20.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses Contribution €=40, Match cap €=60, Match fraction=0.5. What is Employer €?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives 20. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.text: Employees bunch their 401(k) contributions exactly at the employer-match cap (Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Metrick, 2002).
sourceProvenance.pointer: 500-behavioral-economics-findings.md entry 333: k; Choi, Laibson, Madrian & Metrick, 2002
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Distinguish the incentive schedule's kink from a complete retirement decision.
